    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hours after detonating 4.4 tons of lead azide in Iowa, officials reported early test results from the surrounding areas.

    Hours after detonating 4.4 tons of lead azide in Iowa, officials reported early test results from the surrounding areas.

    In a recent development, saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before promptly dissipating.

    Sources indicate that following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” stated Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press.

    According to recent reports, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here.

    Recent findings suggest that the Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.

    According to recent reports, ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.

    Recent findings suggest that to reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army stated it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

    You can schedule WhatsApp texts you might forget to send up to two weeks ahead of time.﻿.

    It has been revealed that whatsApp’s 3 billion users are getting an option that Meta states is one of the most requested features, with the ability to schedule messages in advance for both private conversations and group chats. Most messaging platforms have had this for a very long time, but now it’s on WhatsApp too.

    According to recent reports, if you think of a text at an inconvenient time or don’t want to forget to fire off a birthday message at 4AM, you can draft it and set it to send anywhere from 10 minutes to two weeks later. The feature works with photos and videos, too.

    In a recent development, to schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

    Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

    According to recent reports, scheduled messages work with text, photos and videos, and are rolling out globally over the coming weeks. It’s one more way to show up for the people who matter to you, now at exactly the right time.

    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    FCC approves SpaceX proposal to put AI data centers in space

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (532 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.
    • According to recent reports, the FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences.
    • The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

    According to recent reports, the FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also noted the proposal “risks real harm.”.

    The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

    FCC Chair Brendan Carr noted in a statement that the action “opens a bold fresh frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”.

    According to recent reports, musk thanked Carr in a post on X, writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”.

    This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

    SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

    The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s looks to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document.

    It has been revealed that spaceX has said it aims to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

    The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.
